normalized.governing_thought: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Put the money into the software business instead
executive_summary: Our own data says the orders lose money. At the median of the 14 dark stores our software already runs, each order loses $6.17 after store costs ($2.67 before them). Even the best observed value for every input, combined, still loses $1.76. No site has ever achieved that combination.

The plan needs four records broken at once. The founders' +$2.02 per order needs a $45 average order, 3.5 orders per rider-hour, 1,800 orders a day and promotions at 2%. Each is beyond anything a site has achieved. The Columbus pop-up fell short of the benchmark median on all four, losing $12.57 per order.

It breaks the cash rule even if it works. Spending $9.5M of $12.0M leaves $2.5M at month 18. That is about 6 months of runway at today's burn, half the 12-month floor. At median economics, nine stores would lose ~$18M a year, and a new round is 'unlikely'.

Software is the cheaper way to catch the same growth. Nine late-stage deals are worth $0.86M ARR (+21%), at 81% gross margin, for $0.8M a year of hires. Pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, which is something we can sell them rather than compete with.
Decisions asked of the board: (1) decline Parcelbird Now as proposed; (2) approve ~$0.8M a year for software hiring; (3) agree the evidence that would reopen the operator question (p. 12).

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing ~40% a year, but the operators already in it lose money on every order

claims.claim: Growth is real.
evidence: Compound growth 2022–25: 42% a year, consistent with the founders' 'over 40%'

claims.claim: Profit is not.
evidence: Zipcart (national), 2025: revenue $1,200M, EBITDA −$310M, EBITDA margin −26%, contribution per order −$1.90
QuickBasket (regional), 2025: revenue $210M, EBITDA −$96M, EBITDA margin −46%, contribution per order −$3.40

claims.claim: The national leader, at $1.2B of revenue, still loses $1.90 on the average order.
The one regional operator closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.
'Nobody owns the Midwest' may say more about the economics than about an open opportunity.

slides.title: At the median of the 14 dark stores our software runs, each order loses $6.17, and $2.67 even before paying for the store

claims.claim: Contribution per order at benchmark-median inputs
evidence: Goods margin (27% × $34) +$9.18
Delivery fee +$1.99
Picking & packing −$3.10
Payment & packaging −$1.30
Promotions (6% of AOV) −$2.04
Before store cost −$2.67
Store cost (900 a day) −$3.50
After store cost −$6.17

claims.claim: The software edge is already in these numbers: these 14 stores run on Parcelbird software. Running our own stores would not add an advantage they lack.
Rider cost alone sinks the order
evidence: At $7.40, riders cost more than the goods margin after picking ($6.08)
To break even before store costs at a $34 order would take 3.75 orders per rider-hour. The observed range is 1.9–3.0.

claims.claim: Each plan input against what has actually been seen
evidence: Average order: median $34; best seen $42; plan $45; plan vs best +7%
Orders/rider-hour: median 2.4; best 3.0 (1.9–3.0); plan 3.5; +17%
Orders/site/day: median 900; best 1,400 (400–1,400); plan 1,800; +29%
Promotions: median 6%; best 6%; plan 2%; ⅓ of best

claims.claim: The best order value and the best density came from different sites. No site has achieved both.
The plan survives missing any one target, but it needs all four together, at levels no site has reached, in cities where density is the biggest open question (§12).
evidence: +$0.22 to +$1.52 per order

evidence: That is worth about $20M a year across nine stores

slides.title: Our own Columbus pop-up fell short of the benchmark median on all four drivers the plan depends on

evidence: Average order value: $31 / $34 / $45
Promotions, % of AOV: 12% / 6% / 2%
Orders per rider-hour: 2.1 / 2.4 / 3.5
Orders per site per day: 280 / 900 / 1,800
Contribution / order after store cost: −$12.57 / −$6.17 / +$2.02

At pop-up or median economics, payback never comes

slides.title: The one profitable example, Zipcart's densest city, got there by charging customers more, and lost 14% of its volume

claims.claim: Zipcart contribution per order in its densest city, Q4 2025: +$0.40. This came only after a new $3.99 service fee, promotions cut to 1%, and order volume then fell 14%
evidence: A new $3.99 service fee on every order
Promotions cut to 1% of order value
Order volume in that city then fell 14%
Across the whole company, Zipcart still loses $1.90 per order

claims.claim: Applying Zipcart's levers to our own benchmarks, per order
evidence: Benchmark median: as is −$6.17; with Zipcart levers −$1.05
Best observed on every input: as is −$1.76; with Zipcart levers +$3.97

claims.claim: Pricing is the only lever with evidence behind it, and it is untested here
evidence: At median density, even Zipcart's pricing leaves each order losing about $1.
It works only alongside best-ever order value and density, which no site has combined.
Whether customers keep ordering at higher prices is the open question in §12.

claims.claim: The founders' plan cuts promotions to 2% but adds no service fee. It also assumes volume 29% above the best site, where Zipcart's pricing cost it 14% of its volume.

slides.title: Even on plan, Parcelbird Now breaks the 12-month runway rule. On benchmark economics it would use up the cash

claims.claim: Cash: $12.0M today, −$9.5M plan spend to month 18, $2.5M left at month 18
evidence: 12-month floor at today's $0.4M a month burn: $4.8M
~6 months runway at month 18 if everything goes to plan, half the 12-month floor. That is $2.3M short.

claims.claim: $18.2M a year lost by nine stores at benchmark-median economics, 1.5× all the cash we have
evidence: Losses would be about $1.5M a month

claims.claim: No safety net
evidence: The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator 'unlikely in this market'.
The $9.5M assumes the plan's economics. Any shortfall comes straight out of runway.

slides.title: Two further risks are not priced into the plan: rider pay rules and conflict with our own software customers

claims.claim: Rider pay rules could move against us
evidence: Two of the three launch cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers.
Riders are already the biggest cost per order: $7.40 at the median, $5.07 in the plan.
Every +$1 an hour in rider cost takes $0.29 to $0.42 off each order (plan to median productivity). At the plan's volume across nine stores, that is about $1.7M a year.
The plan has no allowance for this.

claims.claim: Becoming an operator puts us in competition with our customers
evidence: Our benchmark data comes from 14 customer sites. Using it to compete with those customers puts their trust at risk.
Of 37 grocers in the pipeline, several want to launch fast delivery from their own stores. Parcelbird Now would compete with them in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City.
Founder time and engineering would be split between running stores and selling software, just as nine late-stage deals need closing.

claims.claim: Both risks grow with every store we open, and neither is costed in the $9.5M. Better operations cannot remove either of them.

slides.title: The software business is a cheaper way to ride the same growth: nine late-stage deals would add ~21% to ARR for $0.8M a year

claims.claim: Software growth potential
evidence: $0.86M ARR from 9 late-stage deals, +21% on today's $4.1M
$3.55M ARR if all 37 pipeline grocers signed (upper bound)
81% gross margin, on a business already growing 60% a year
$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires, the whole cost

Unit economics: −$6.17 per order at the benchmark median vs 81% gross margin

Exposure to rider pay rules: Direct vs Borne by the grocer

claims.claim: Delivering from grocers' existing stores avoids the $1.15M-a-year dark store. That is the product our pipeline is asking for.
evidence: At median density that store costs $3.50 per order, the biggest single line separating a loss from break-even

slides.title: We ask the board to decline Parcelbird Now for 2027, fund the software plan, and agree what would reopen the question

claims.claim: Decisions for today
evidence: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch (nine dark stores, $9.5M) for 2027.
Approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires, focused on closing the 9 late-stage deals.
Commission a plan for a fast-delivery-from-store module for pipeline grocers, to come to the next board.
Hold cash to the 12-month runway floor. Revisit only through the triggers on the right.

claims.claim: What would reopen the operator question: all three, ideally shown first by a customer's site on our platform, at no cost to us
evidence: Positive contribution after store costs for two quarters in a row at a site in a mid-size city doing 1,400+ orders a day
Evidence that customers accept higher prices, e.g. a service fee test where order volume holds
Funding that keeps 12+ months of runway through the launch, plus clarity on rider pay rules in Indianapolis and Kansas City

claims.claim: Waiting costs us little. Our software already shows us how every customer site performs. If a customer's dark store starts to make money, we will see it early in our own data.

slides.title: Appendix B: judgment calls and limits of this analysis

claims.claim: Definition of contribution: the conclusion holds either way: at the median an order loses money even before the store is paid for.
evidence: The pack does not define the founders' 'contribution profit'. We show results both before and after the dark-store fixed cost.

claims.claim: Cash need: we read the $9.5M as the total company need to month 18, the most favourable reading for the plan.
evidence: If it is on top of today's $0.4M a month burn, the plan needs ~$16.7M, more than the $12.0M in the bank.

claims.claim: Pop-up ramp: the pop-up is evidence on demand and operations, not on mature-store economics.
evidence: Run-rates of ~180 and ~410 orders a day assume steady 18% weekly growth over six weeks
temporary site with a lower $650k fixed cost

claims.claim: Customer payback uses contribution after store cost per order and leaves out orders in months 1–2 and churn after month 3, because the pack has no data on either.
Zipcart comparison applies Zipcart's fee, promotion and volume changes to our benchmarks with every other input unchanged. Zipcart's own definition of contribution is not given.
Not modelled: launch marketing, head-office cost and ramp-up losses (all inside the founders' $9.5M), and close rates on the software pipeline, which the pack does not give.

normalized.recommendation: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch (nine dark stores, $9.5M) for 2027; approve ~$0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires, focused on closing the 9 late-stage deals; commission a plan for a fast-delivery-from-store module for pipeline grocers, to come to the next board; hold cash to the 12-month runway floor and revisit only through the agreed triggers.

alternatives_considered.option: Launch Parcelbird Now (operator): nine dark stores in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City, $9.5M to month 18 (founders' plan)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected for 2027: −$6.17 per order at the benchmark median; plan's +$2.02 needs four assumptions at once, each beyond anything a site has achieved; breaches the 12-month runway rule even on plan (~6 months left); exposure to rider pay rules and competition with software customers.

alternatives_considered.option: Scale the software (supplier): 2 engineers and 2 sales hires to close 9 late-stage deals
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen: ~$0.8M a year, +$0.86M ARR (+21%), 81% gross margin, runway rule kept, supplier to grocers' fast delivery, rider pay exposure borne by the grocer.
Recommended for a plan to come to the next board; avoids the $1.15M-a-year dark store, 'the product our pipeline is asking for'.

alternatives_considered.option: Apply Zipcart's pricing levers ($3.99 service fee, promotions at 1%)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Pricing is the only lever with evidence behind it, but untested here; at median density still loses about $1 per order (−$1.05); Zipcart lost 14% of volume; founders' plan adds no service fee.

Only if all three triggers are met: positive contribution after store costs for two quarters at a 1,400+ orders/day mid-size-city site; evidence customers accept higher prices; funding that keeps 12+ months runway plus clarity on rider pay rules.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: The pack does not define the founders' 'contribution profit'; results shown both before and after the dark-store fixed cost.
The $9.5M is read as the total company need to month 18 (most favourable reading); if it excludes today's $0.4M a month burn, the need is ~$16.7M, more than the cash.

Pop-up run-rates of ~180 and ~410 orders a day assume steady 18% weekly growth over six weeks (11,800 orders total); the pop-up was a temporary site with a $650k annualised fixed cost, so it is evidence on demand and operations, not mature-store economics.
Customer payback counts only contribution after store cost and leaves out orders in months 1–2 and churn after month 3; the pack has no data on either.
Zipcart comparison applies its fee, promotion and volume changes with every other input unchanged; Zipcart's own definition of contribution is not given.
Not modelled: launch marketing, head-office cost and ramp-up losses (inside the founders' $9.5M), and close rates on the software pipeline.
Pipeline values = deals × $96,000 average contract; close rates are not in the pack, so the full pipeline is an upper bound.
Nine-store results are steady state, before launch marketing and head-office cost.
Bridge applies plan inputs one at a time in the order shown; steps may not sum exactly due to rounding.
Best observed values for each input came from different sites; no site has combined them.
Density in the launch cities is the biggest open question (§12); whether customers keep ordering at higher prices is open.
Two of the three launch cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers; not costed in the plan.
The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator 'unlikely in this market'.

normalized.extraction_notes: The deck arrived as extracted plain text with no images. Chart values were rebuilt from the flattened text labels. Bar-to-category matches were inferred from their order: the GMV-by-year chart on slide 3, the waterfall on slide 4, the bridge on slide 5 and the cash waterfall on slide 9. The ordering on slide 5 is the least certain. On slide 7, the callout figures (18%, 12%, 22%, $38) were paired with their descriptions based on how the text was interleaved. On slide 8, the +$0.40 figure is read as Zipcart's densest-city contribution. Slide numbers and section labels were left out of the claims.
